title: Plan the strategy and logistic requirements for work site pest management interventions

lessons.title: Developing the intervention strategy
lessons.html:
From findings to strategy

The inspection and impact assessment tell you what the problem is. The strategy sets out how you will solve it. A good strategy is targeted, legal, safe, effective and acceptable to the client.

Define the objective

State a measurable objective agreed with the client, for example: eliminate German cockroach activity in the kitchen within six weeks; disinfest 2 000 tons of maize in bins 4 to 7 before outloading; clear Category 1b wattle from the riparian strip and achieve at least 90 percent kill at the first follow-up.

Select methods

  1. List all feasible options: sanitation, proofing, trapping, baiting, spraying, dusting, fumigation, physical treatments such as heat or cooling, and biological control.
  2. Evaluate each for effectiveness against the pest and life stages present, risk to people and environment, site constraints, timing, cost and client acceptability.
  3. Select a combination, using the least hazardous effective approach.

Select products

  • Confirm each product is registered under Act 36 of 1947 for the pest and situation, and check the label for dose, application method, restrictions, re-entry and withholding periods.
  • Consider formulation: gels and baits in sensitive areas; residual sprays for perimeter work; fumigants only where gas-tightness can be achieved.
  • Consider resistance history and rotate chemical groups.
  • Obtain SDSs for the risk assessment.

Risk assessment

Prepare a job-specific risk assessment covering workers, occupants, neighbours, food and product, animals, water and other environmental receptors. Identify controls: timing out of hours, evacuation, exclusion zones, PPE, signage, notifications and emergency arrangements.

Client responsibilities

Specify what the client must do, such as cleaning, emptying cupboards, removing pets, repairing proofing, isolating equipment or stopping intake. Agree dates. Many failures happen because these tasks are not completed.

lessons.title: Calculating quantities and resources
lessons.html:
Quantities

Accurate calculations prevent under-treatment, waste and stock shortages on the day.

Typical calculations

  • Area treatments: measure the area in square metres and apply the label rate and your calibrated application volume to calculate product and water needed.
  • Volume treatments: calculate the volume of rooms, structures or enclosures in cubic metres for space treatments and fumigation (length x width x height; for cylindrical bins, use the area of the circle times the height).
  • Commodity treatments: use tonnage where the label dose is per ton.
  • Bait and trap numbers: based on site plan, perimeter length and label or company spacing guidelines.

Always double-check calculations and have a colleague or supervisor verify doses for fumigation and large treatments.

Worked example

A rectangular warehouse measures 40 m by 20 m with a 6 m height. Its volume is 40 x 20 x 6 = 4 800 cubic metres. If a space treatment label specified a rate per 100 cubic metres, you would divide 4 800 by 100 and multiply by that rate. The actual rate always comes from the product label.

Resources

ResourcePlanning questions
PeopleHow many, which registrations and skills, who supervises, who is standby?
ProductsQuantity in stock, ordering lead time, storage on site
EquipmentSprayers, foggers, fumigation sheets, gas monitors, respirators; calibrated and serviced?
PPECorrect types and sizes, cartridges in date, fit tested
TransportVehicle suitable for safe chemical transport, spill kit
ConsumablesTape, sand snakes, signage, bait stations, labels

lessons.title: Scheduling, communication and the work plan
lessons.html:
Scheduling

Plan the timing around the pest, the product and the client:

  • Pest biology: treat when the vulnerable stage is present; schedule follow-ups to catch hatching eggs.
  • Product needs: minimum temperatures and exposure periods for fumigants, dry weather for outdoor sprays, active growth for systemic herbicides.
  • Client operations: production shutdowns, harvest intake peaks, school holidays, guest occupancy.
  • Re-entry and withholding periods: allow time before occupation or product release.

Communication plan

  1. Send the client a written proposal or work plan with objectives, methods, products, schedule, preparation requirements, precautions and costs.
  2. Obtain written approval before starting.
  3. Prepare notices for occupants and neighbours where required.
  4. Brief your team at a toolbox talk on the plan, roles, hazards and emergency procedures.

Contingency planning

Plan for weather changes, equipment failure, client preparation not done, unexpected occupants, spills and exposures, and gas leaks in fumigation. Decide in advance who can stop or postpone the job.

The written work plan

A complete plan includes site details, objective, pest and extent, methods and products with registration numbers and calculated quantities, risk assessment and controls, resources, schedule, client responsibilities, communication, monitoring and evaluation, and contingencies. It becomes the reference for the team and evidence of due diligence.

Key points

  • Set a measurable objective and select the least hazardous effective combination of methods.
  • Use only products registered for the pest and situation and follow the label.
  • Calculate area, volume or tonnage accurately and verify doses for high-risk treatments.
  • Plan people, products, equipment, PPE and transport in advance.
  • Schedule around pest biology, product requirements and client operations, and get written approval.
